The ceiling fan slowed, groaned and stopped just as Ammi lifted the pressure cooker off the stove. It was eleven in the morning in June, and the whole of our street in Gujranwala went silent at once.

At first we treated it like an ordinary load-shedding hour. My younger brother Hamza opened the fridge to "save the ice", Abbu checked the UPS, which beeped twice and died, and I sat on the stairs refreshing my phone until the battery dropped to twelve per cent. By two o'clock the transformer on the corner had a crowd of neighbours under it, and someone from the electricity office said it would take "until evening, maybe".

The afternoon was the hardest part. The rooms grew so hot that we carried charpais into the courtyard under the neem tree. Hamza complained loudly. I complained silently, which was worse. Then Dadi, who had said almost nothing all day, asked me to fetch the old hand fan from the steel trunk. While she fanned herself, she began telling us about summers in her village, when the only cold thing in the house was a clay pitcher wrapped in wet cloth.

"We used to wait for the evening breeze like a guest," she said. Hamza stopped sulking and asked how they slept. Abbu laughed and admitted he had slept on the roof until he was fifteen. Ammi brought out the cooled daal and rotis, and we ate in the courtyard, passing one torch between us like a microphone.

The lights came back at half past nine. The fans roared, the television switched itself on and everyone hurried indoors. I stayed outside a moment longer.

I had expected to remember that day as the day nothing worked. Instead I remember it as the day I heard my grandmother's childhood for the first time. We live in the same house, yet it took ten hours of darkness for us to actually sit together and listen.

The Tezgam was supposed to leave Rawalpindi at half past seven in the morning. My cousin Fahad and I had planned every hour of the trip to Lahore: lunch at Jhelum, a nap after Gujrat, and arrival in time for our aunt's mehndi that evening.

The train left forty minutes late, which we expected. What we did not expect was the long, shuddering stop in the middle of the fields beyond Lala Musa. Ten minutes passed, then an hour. A guard walking along the track told us an engine ahead had broken down and that we would wait "until the relief engine comes".

Fahad called his mother three times. I sat with my feet on our suitcase, calculating how many dances we would miss. The carriage grew hot, and a baby two seats away began to cry without stopping.

Then an elderly man opposite us opened a tiffin carrier and offered us parathas. "Travel is like this," he said calmly. "You reach when you reach." His name was Rana Sahib, and he had been taking this route for forty years. He told us about the time floods had kept him on a train for two days, and about the stranger who had shared his blanket that night.

Slowly, the carriage changed. Someone produced a thermos of tea. A university student played cricket commentary on his phone for the boys in the next compartment. Fahad, who had been sulking, ended up holding the crying baby while her tired mother drank her tea.

The relief engine arrived after four hours. We reached Lahore at nine at night, sweaty and crumpled, and walked into the mehndi just as the final song began. Our aunt laughed at our faces and pulled us straight into the circle.

I still make plans for every journey, but now I pack an extra packet of biscuits and a little more patience. The most memorable part of that trip was not where we were going, but the strangers we met while we were stuck.

The red ink on my chemistry test said 14 out of 50. I folded the paper twice before anyone in the row could see it, but my face had already told them.

It had started three weeks earlier. Our teacher, Sir Naveed, had announced the test on organic reactions, and I had decided I did not need to prepare early. I had done well in the first term, and I believed I could learn everything in the last two nights. So I spent the evenings watching match highlights and helping my friend Usman edit videos for his channel.

Two nights before the test, I opened my notes and found thirty reactions, each with conditions and products I barely recognised. I stayed up until three, drank too much tea, and fell asleep with the book on my chest. The next night the electricity went, and my phone torch died at midnight. I walked into the test tired, confused and pretending to be confident.

After class, Sir Naveed called me to his desk. I expected anger. Instead he asked quietly, "When did you start revising?" I wanted to blame the load-shedding, but I told him the truth. He nodded and said, "Talent gets you started. Habits get you finished."

That evening I made a simple timetable: forty minutes of chemistry every day, a short self-test every Sunday, and match highlights only after both were done. It felt boring at first. By the end of the month, though, I could write the reactions without looking, and the retest came back with 41.

The mark was not the real lesson. The lesson was that confidence without preparation is just a gamble, and I had bet my own future on it. Now, whenever I feel sure I can "manage later", I remember the red 14 and open my notes that day.

"Just send the photo. Everyone else has," Sana whispered, holding her phone under the desk.

It was the night before our final English paper, and someone had shared what looked like the question paper in our class group. By the time I saw it, forty messages had appeared beneath it: laughing faces, thank-yous, and plans to "just memorise the essay". My best friends, Sana and Maryam, had already written their answers.

I stared at the blurry picture for a long time. Part of me wanted to look. I had worked hard all year, but English was my weakest subject, and my father had told everyone at the dinner table that I would get an A. Another part of me remembered my mother marking papers at the kitchen table for her own students, sighing whenever she found copied work.

"If it's fake, you lose nothing," Maryam texted. "If it's real, you lose everything by not looking."

I turned the phone face down and opened my essay notes instead. I did not sleep well. At school the next morning, Sana asked whether I had seen it. When I said no, she rolled her eyes and walked away to sit with the others.

The paper turned out to be completely different. The leaked picture had been from another board's old exam. Half the class came out pale and silent. I had not done brilliantly, but I had written about a topic I had practised, in my own words.

Sana did not speak to me for two days. On the third, she sat beside me at break and said, "You were annoying, but you were right." We laughed, though both of us knew it had been close.

The paper's being fake was luck. Refusing to look was not. I learned that the hardest choices are the small, quiet ones made alone at night, with nobody watching except yourself.

The old woman was standing at the edge of Murree Road with a plastic bag in each hand, watching the traffic as if it were a river she could not swim.

I was on my way back from the academy in Saddar, tired and thinking only about dinner. Cars, wagons and motorbikes rushed past her without slowing. She stepped forward, then back. A rickshaw horn made her drop one bag, and oranges rolled into the gutter.

For a second I hesitated. I was not sure she would want help from a stranger, and I worried about looking foolish. Then one orange rolled to my shoe, and that decided it. I picked it up, then the others, and put them back in her bag.

"Amma ji, where are you going?" I asked.

"To the hospital on the other side," she said. "My son is admitted. I came on the wagon but I don't know these roads." Her voice was steady, but her hands were shaking.

I took both bags, held her arm and waited for a gap. When a traffic warden noticed us, he raised his hand and stopped the cars, and we crossed slowly together. On the far side, I asked which ward her son was in. She showed me a crumpled slip of paper, so I walked her through the gate, past the crowded reception, up to the second floor.

Her son was sitting up in bed with a bandaged leg. When he saw his mother, he tried to stand, and she scolded him like a schoolboy. Then she turned to me and insisted I take two oranges. I tried to refuse; she would not hear of it.

I was forty minutes late home and my mother wanted an explanation. When I gave it, she said nothing, but she put extra salan on my plate.

The help I gave took less than an hour. What stayed with me was how close I came to walking past. Now, when I notice someone struggling, I try not to wait for an orange to roll to my feet.

Nobody in the house noticed that the front door was open. It was the evening before Eid, and the Qureshi house in Multan was full of noise: the pressure cooker hissing, cousins arguing over mehndi designs, and Uncle Javed shouting into his phone about a delayed bus.

Only Zainab, who was nine, noticed that Moti was missing. The small white goat had been tied by the courtyard wall for a week, eating chopped grass and the occasional dupatta. Now the rope lay empty on the bricks.

"Moti's gone!" she cried. Nobody heard her the first time. The second time, she climbed onto a chair and shouted it, and the whole house fell silent.

Within minutes the street was full of Qureshis. Uncle Javed ran towards the main road. The older cousins checked the empty plot behind the mosque. Zainab's grandfather, who walked with a stick, went slowly from door to door asking the neighbours. Zainab followed him, holding his hand and trying not to cry.

They had almost given up when they reached the house of Mrs Bano, a widow who lived alone at the end of the lane. Her door was half open too. Inside, in her tiny courtyard, Moti was calmly eating the leaves of her potted plant while Mrs Bano sat on the step, laughing for the first time anyone could remember.

"He came in by himself," she said. "I thought perhaps Allah had sent me a guest for Eid."

Zainab's grandfather looked at the lonely little courtyard, then at Zainab. Something passed between them without words.

The next afternoon, after the prayers, the Qureshis carried a large dish of food down the lane, and Mrs Bano joined them for the meal, sitting beside Zainab. Moti had gone back home on his rope, but from that Eid on, the Qureshis made sure that one door in the lane was always open for her.

On the first day of college I walked confidently into Room 12, sat in the second row and opened my new physics notebook. The lecturer wrote "Introduction to Fine Arts" on the board.

I had read the timetable wrong. Physics was in Room 21, on the other side of the building. My face turned hot, but the lecturer, Miss Rubina, had already begun the attendance, and leaving felt more embarrassing than staying. So I stayed.

She handed everyone a sheet of paper and a charcoal stick. "Draw your hand," she said. "Not the hand you think you have. The one in front of you." I had not drawn anything since primary school, when I coloured mountains brown and the sky blue. My first lines were stiff and wrong. Miss Rubina stopped beside me, looked at the drawing and said, "You're looking at the paper. Look at your hand." I tried again, and slowly the knuckles and wrinkles appeared.

When the class ended, I explained my mistake. She laughed. "Physics will still be there tomorrow," she said. "Come on Thursday if you like. Art is free for anyone who turns up."

I went on Thursday, and the Thursday after that. My parents thought it was a waste of time at first, especially my father, who wanted me to be an engineer. I kept going to physics too, and I did well, but the Thursday class became the part of the week I looked forward to most. Drawing taught me patience and close observation, and strangely, it helped my diagrams in physics practicals.

Three years later, I chose architecture, a subject that needed both maths and drawing. My father came to my first exhibition at the university and stood in front of my sketch of the old Haveli in Lahore for a long time. Every time I think about that wrong room, I smile. It was the best mistake I ever made.

I had ironed my best shalwar kameez the night before, but by the time we reached the school hall in Hyderabad, the sweat had already ruined it. Nobody looked at the fathers anyway. They looked at the stage.

My daughter Hira had told me nothing except that I must come. "Just come, Abbu," she had said. "Don't ask." I sat near the back, on a plastic chair that wobbled, beside mothers taking photographs and a grandfather who kept falling asleep.

The headmistress spoke for a long time about discipline. Then the prizes began: best in mathematics, best in Urdu, best attendance. Each name was followed by clapping and the flash of phones. I did not hear Hira's name and I told myself it did not matter. She had been ill for two months in the winter, and I knew she had struggled to catch up. I had sometimes sat beside her at midnight while she copied notes from her friends, because I could not help her with chemistry myself. I never finished school. I drive a rickshaw.

Near the end, the headmistress said there was one more award, chosen by the teachers: for the student who had shown the greatest determination this year. She smiled, paused, and read out, "Hira Bashir."

I did not stand up straight away. The grandfather next to me nudged me, and I realised I was crying in front of three hundred people. Hira walked onto the stage, took the certificate, and looked into the audience until she found me. She did not wave. She just held the certificate a little higher.

Afterwards, in the car park, she handed it to me. "It's yours too," she said. "You were awake every night."

The certificate now hangs above our television, in a frame that cost more than I like to admit. When customers ask about it, I tell them it is my daughter's. Then I tell them it is a little bit mine.

The website was supposed to show the matric results at ten o'clock. At five past ten it showed a spinning circle. At twenty past, it showed an error message.

I had woken at six, prayed Fajr and then sat on the bed doing nothing. My mother made my favourite aloo parathas, which made me more nervous, because she only made them on special days. My little sister kept asking, "Are you going to fail?" until Ammi sent her to the neighbours.

By eleven, the whole family was in the small lounge of our flat in Karachi. My father had taken half a day off from the bank. My uncle phoned twice to ask for my roll number. Every time someone's phone buzzed, my heart did too. Finally my cousin Rehan, who knew the trick of sending the roll number by SMS, said, "Give it to me."

The reply took three minutes. Rehan read it silently, and his face showed nothing. "Read it," my father said.

"Nine hundred and eighty-seven," Rehan said slowly. "Out of eleven hundred."

For a moment nobody moved. I had been hoping for nine hundred, and secretly afraid of eight. Then my mother made a sound that was half laugh and half cry, and my father put his hand on my head the way he had when I was small. My sister burst in from next door, shouting that she had known all along.

The rest of the day was a blur of mithai boxes, phone calls and relatives who had never asked about my studies suddenly asking for my study timetable. In the evening, I sat alone on the balcony looking at the traffic on Shahrah-e-Faisal.

I felt proud, but I also felt something I had not expected: relief that my parents' sacrifices had not been wasted. The marks were mine, but the day belonged to all of us.

We left Islamabad before dawn, five of us squeezed into my uncle's old Suzuki with a cooler of water bottles and a bag of samosas that were cold before Hasan Abdal. I had grown up in the plains and had seen the northern mountains only on calendars.

After Abbottabad the road began to climb. The air coming through the window changed from dusty and warm to sharp and green. My cousin Areeba pressed her face against the glass every time the river appeared below us, grey and foaming. Near Balakot, we stopped at a dhaba where the chai came in thick glasses and tasted of smoke. A boy no older than ten served us, counting our change faster than I could.

The road through the Kaghan Valley was narrower than I had imagined. In places the mountain rose straight up on one side and fell away on the other. Uncle Tariq drove slowly, humming old songs to hide his nerves. Twice we waited while flocks of sheep crossed, their shepherd waving a stick and smiling.

We reached Naran in the afternoon, tired and stiff. The next morning we took a jeep up to Lake Saiful Muluk. I had heard about the lake for years and expected to be impressed. I did not expect to go completely silent. The water was so still that the snowy peak of Malika Parbat lay upside down in it, perfect and enormous. Even Areeba, who had talked for the whole journey, simply stood and stared.

An old boatman told us the legend of the prince and the fairy, and we listened like children.

On the way home, I kept thinking how close all this had been. For seventeen years, I had lived a day's drive from such beauty and had never seen it. I promised myself that I would not need a calendar to show me my own country again.

My grandfather's hands were covered in tiny scars, each one, he said, from a different shoe.

He had been a cobbler in the old city of Peshawar for fifty years, in a shop so narrow that two customers could not stand side by side. The summer I was fifteen, my father sent me to help him for a month. I went unwillingly. I wanted to spend the holidays playing football and gaming with my friends, not sitting on a low stool among glue pots and leather.

On the first day, Nana Jan gave me a pair of worn sandals and told me to stitch the strap. I finished in ten minutes, pleased with myself. He tugged the strap once and it came loose. "Again," he said. I did it again, faster. He pulled it off again. By the fourth attempt, I was angry.

"Why does it matter?" I said. "It's a cheap sandal. He'll buy a new one next year."

Nana Jan put down his awl and looked at me. "That man is a labourer," he said. "He walks ten kilometres a day in these. If the strap breaks on the road, he walks barefoot on hot stones. You are not stitching a sandal. You are stitching his day."

I said nothing. On the fifth attempt I went slowly, pulling every stitch tight, checking the knot twice. He tugged the strap hard, nodded and put the sandal on the shelf without a word. That silence felt like a medal.

For the rest of the month I learned to resole shoes, fix zips and polish leather until it shone. I also learned the names of his customers and the stories behind their shoes.

Nana Jan died two years later. I am studying to be a civil engineer now, and when I check a calculation for the third time, my friends tease me. I don't mind. Somewhere, someone will walk across what I build.

The cricket ball had gone straight through the Malik family's front window, and only Daniyal and I had seen who hit it.

It was a Friday afternoon in our street in Sialkot. Six of us were playing with a taped tennis ball, which was safe enough, until Saad brought out a hard ball his uncle had bought from the factory. On the first over I swung wildly, and the crack of glass seemed to stop the whole street. The others scattered. Daniyal and I hid behind a parked car.

Within minutes, Uncle Malik was standing at his gate, his face red. "Who did this?" he shouted. Then he saw his own son's bicycle near the wicket and assumed it was Faizan, who had been watching from the roof and was not even playing.

Daniyal grabbed my arm. "Don't say anything," he whispered. "He'll just think Faizan did it. Your father will kill you."

He was right about my father. A new window would cost several thousand rupees, and Abbu had been worried about money all month. For a moment, keeping quiet felt sensible. Then I heard Faizan, inside the house, crying and saying, "It wasn't me, I swear."

I stood up before I could change my mind. My legs felt like rubber. "Uncle, it was me," I said. "I'm sorry. I'll pay for it."

He stared at me, then at the broken glass. His anger seemed to drain away. "At least someone in this street has a spine," he muttered.

My father did not kill me. He was angry, and he took the money for the glass from my savings, which hurt. But that evening, he told my mother the whole story at dinner, and I noticed he did not sound angry at all.

Faizan and I became friends after that. I learned that a lie might save you once, but it always costs someone else. The truth cost me my savings, but I could look at Faizan without shame.

Every morning, Kashif sat in the last row of our class in Bahawalpur with his English book open at the same page. He had joined in the middle of the year from a village school, and whenever Miss Nadia asked him to read aloud, the room filled with giggles.

For weeks I laughed too. Then one day I saw him at the bus stop, moving his lips silently over a newspaper headline, trying to sound out the words. He looked up, saw me and shoved the paper into his bag. I felt ashamed in a way I could not explain.

The next day I sat next to him at break. "I could help you read, if you want," I said. He shrugged, but he didn't say no.

We began with the stories in our textbook. I read a line, then he read it after me. He stumbled over words like "though" and "enough", and I realised for the first time how strange English spelling is. We made a list of tricky words in a notebook, and every day he added five more. By the third week, he was reading whole paragraphs, slowly but correctly.

Then he started helping me. Kashif was brilliant at mathematics. He could solve problems in his head that took me half a page. "You read for me, I'll do sums for you," he said, grinning. Our break times turned into a small, noisy study session, and soon two other boys joined us.

The real turning point came in March. Miss Nadia asked Kashif to read a passage in front of the class. Nobody giggled. He read the whole page, and when he finished, she said, "Very good, Kashif." He did not look at me, but his ears turned red with pride.

I started helping him because I felt guilty. I kept going because I discovered that teaching someone else was the best way to understand a subject myself. And I gained a friend I would never have known if I had kept laughing.

My father answered on the fourth ring. I heard him say, "Ji? Kahan?" in a voice I had never heard before, and then he was pulling on his jacket over his kurta. My mother stood in the doorway holding her dupatta to her mouth.

"It's your Chacha," Abbu said. "His car has gone off the road near Kuchlak. He's at the hospital." He looked at me. "You're coming. I can't drive and use the phone."

Outside, the cold was so sharp it hurt my teeth. The streets were empty except for a few trucks and stray dogs. Abbu sat beside me making calls while I drove our old car as carefully as I could. I had only had my licence for three months. My hands were sweating on the steering wheel despite the cold.

At the hospital, the corridor smelt of disinfectant. A nurse led us to a room, and there was Chacha Imran, sitting on the bed with a bandage on his forehead and a cup of tea in his hand.

"Why have you all come?" he said, surprised. "I told the policeman to call and say I'm fine!"

It turned out that the policeman had dialled our number, said "accident" and "hospital", and then the line had dropped. Chacha had swerved to avoid a camel on the road and ended up in a shallow ditch. His car was dented, but he had only a cut.

Abbu sat down heavily on the chair and laughed until his eyes were wet. Then he hugged his brother for a long time.

We drove home as the sky turned pink over the mountains. Abbu was quiet, then said, "You drove well tonight." It was a small sentence, but I knew it meant he trusted me now.

His father was getting older. His knees hurt on the cold mornings, and his eyes were not as sharp as they had been. Sameer had worked on the boat every summer since he was twelve. Everyone at the harbour assumed that one day the Noor-e-Sahar would be his.

My father and I joined a group of men forming a human chain across the lane. The water was cold and full of floating rubbish. I carried a little girl on my shoulders while her mother clung to my arm. The admission form lay on the table between my parents and me like a chessboard. One box had to be ticked: pre-medical, pre-engineering, ICS or commerce.

Everyone in our family in Rawalakot assumed I would choose pre-medical. My elder brother was in his fourth year at a medical college. My mother had always called me "our little doctor". At family weddings, aunties asked, "When will she wear the white coat?"

The trouble was that I hated biology. I could memorise it, but it never excited me. What excited me was the old computer in our school laboratory, where I had taught myself to write small programs during free periods. I had made a simple quiz game for my class and a timetable app for my friends. When the program worked, I felt the way my brother said he felt when he understood a diagnosis.

"Computer science is not a stable career," my father said when I raised it. "Doctors are always needed."

My mother was quieter. "Are you sure this is not just a hobby?"

I wasn't sure. So I asked my computer teacher, Sir Ijaz, for advice. He didn't tell me what to choose. Instead he asked me to explain one of my programs to him. I talked for twenty minutes without stopping. He smiled. "That," he said, "is not what a hobby sounds like."

That night, I sat with my parents and showed them the quiz game and the app. I explained what software engineers did and the universities in Pakistan that taught it. My father asked many questions. Some I could answer; some I couldn't.

Finally he picked up the pen and handed it to me. "It's your form," he said.

I ticked ICS. Two years later, I am preparing for university entry tests in computer science, and I have never once regretted it. The choice was mine, but my parents' trust made it possible.

prompt: Write about a time you helped an animal in trouble.
task: Write a narrative of about 250-350 words in the first person. Describe how you found the animal, what you did step by step, and what the experience meant to you.

Makes the setting specific

Tells the rescue or care in a clear sequence

model:
The kitten was wedged inside the drain pipe outside our house in Gulberg, crying so loudly that it sounded like a baby.

It had rained all night, and water was still trickling through the pipe. I could see one small grey paw and two terrified eyes. I was on my way to the academy, already late, and my first thought was that someone else would deal with it. Then the trickle of water grew stronger, and the crying became desperate.

I dropped my bag and knelt in the mud. The pipe was too narrow for my hand. "Ammi!" I shouted. My mother came out with her dupatta over her head and looked at the pipe. "Get the oil," she said at once.

I ran inside for the cooking oil. Our neighbour, Uncle Khalid, came over too, holding a torch and a flat piece of wood. We poured a little oil around the edge of the pipe. Uncle Khalid slid the wood under the kitten to stop it slipping further. Very slowly, I wrapped my fingers around its paw and pulled while my mother held the pipe steady.

With a wet squeak, the kitten came out. It was thin, shaking and covered in mud and oil. It scratched my wrist and then clung to my shirt as if it would never let go.

My mother wrapped it in an old towel and warmed some milk. My little brother named it Badal, meaning cloud, because it was grey. I phoned the academy and explained why I was late. My teacher laughed and said it was the most original excuse she had heard all year.

Badal is a fat, lazy cat now and sleeps on top of the fridge. My mother pretends she doesn't like him, but I often catch her saving pieces of chicken for him.

The scratch on my wrist faded in a week. The lesson didn't: when something small cries for help, don't wait for someone else.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the sentence: "When the lights came back on, the old man had disappeared."

model:
When the lights came back on, the old man had disappeared. A moment earlier he had been sitting in the corner of the waiting room at Rohri Junction, a thin figure wrapped in a brown blanket, a cloth bundle on his knees. Now there was only the empty bench.

It was past midnight, and the train to Karachi was three hours late. The power had failed for barely five minutes. The other passengers, a family with sleeping children and two students with headphones, hardly noticed. But I had been watching him, because earlier he had asked me, in a soft Saraiki voice, which platform the Quetta train left from. I had told him I didn't know.

On the bench, where he had been, lay his bundle.

I picked it up and went outside. The platform was dim and almost deserted. A tea seller was folding his stall. "Did you see an old man in a brown blanket?" I asked. He pointed towards the far end of the platform, where the tracks curved away into the dark.

I followed. Past the last lamp, a goods train was standing on a side line. And there, sitting on the edge of the platform, was the old man, staring at the empty tracks.

"You left this," I said, holding out the bundle.

He looked at it for a long moment. "It's for my grandson," he said. "In Quetta. A sweater. My daughter knitted it before she died." He told me he had missed his train four hours earlier and had been too ashamed to ask for help again.

I went to the station master's office. The official checked his ticket, stamped it for the next morning's train and gave him permission to wait in the staff room, which had a heater.

When my train finally arrived, I looked back. The old man was holding his bundle on his lap, warm, waiting, no longer lost.

The key is iron, longer than my hand, and so heavy that it pulls down any pocket you put it in. It belonged to my grandfather's shop in the walled city of Lahore, near Delhi Gate.

The shop sold spices. As a small boy, I would sit on a sack of red chillies while Nana Abbu weighed out cumin, turmeric and cardamom for his customers. Every evening at eight, he pulled down the wooden shutters and locked them with that key, turning it three times. "Once for the shop, once for the family, once for Allah's protection," he always said.

When I was twelve, the shop was sold. Nana Abbu was getting old, and my uncles had jobs in Islamabad and Dubai. Nobody wanted to sit among the spice sacks any more. On the last evening, he let me lock the shutters myself. My small hands could barely turn the key. When I did, he patted my head and put the key in his own pocket.

He lived with us after that, in our flat in Johar Town. He became quiet. He missed the noise of the bazaar, the smells, the customers who called him "Haji Sahib". Sometimes I saw him sitting by the window, turning the key over in his hands.

Before he passed away, when I was sixteen, he called me to his bed and pressed the key into my palm. "The shop is gone," he said. "But what it taught you is not. Honest weights. Fair prices. Greeting everyone the same, rich or poor." He closed my fingers over it. "Lock those things in yourself."

I am at university now, studying business. When I am tempted to cut corners, to exaggerate on a project or take a shortcut, I feel the heavy key in my bag and remember the three turns. And that is why I still keep the old key.

At two in the morning, the emergency ward of the district hospital in Sheikhupura is never quiet. Fans whir, a child coughs, a relative argues with the guard at the door. I had been on duty for fourteen hours and was drinking my fourth cup of tea when the ambulance siren came screaming into the yard.

The patient was a man in his forties, brought in by his son after a motorbike accident on the motorway. He was pale, sweating and barely conscious. His blood pressure was dropping. My senior, Dr Farooq, was in theatre with another case. For a moment, I was the most senior doctor in the room. I was twenty-five years old.

My hands knew what to do before my mind caught up. "Two lines, fluids, cross-match blood," I said to the nurse, Sister Rukhsana, who had worked there for twenty years. She was already doing it. I examined his abdomen; it was hard and swollen. Internal bleeding, I thought. He needed surgery quickly.

I called Dr Farooq. "Keep him stable for twenty minutes," he said. "I'm closing." Twenty minutes felt like twenty hours. The son stood in the corner, gripping his cap, asking again and again, "Will Abba be all right?" I told him we were doing everything we could, which was true, and that I didn't know, which was also true.

The blood arrived. His pressure rose slowly. At exactly the twenty-second minute, Dr Farooq hurried in, still in his theatre cap, examined him and nodded. "Good work. Theatre, now."

The surgery took three hours. At dawn, Dr Farooq came out and told the son that his father would live. The young man burst into tears and touched my arm. "Thank you, Doctor Sahib."

I went outside to the hospital courtyard and watched the sun come up over the wall. My hands were finally shaking. I realised that I had not been brave, only trained. Tonight, that had been enough.

model:
My grandmother, Nani Amma, wakes at four every morning, and on the day I stayed with her in her village near Chiniot, so did I, very unwillingly.

She had already prayed and lit the clay stove in the courtyard by the time I stumbled out of bed. The sky was still dark, and the air smelt of smoke and wet earth. "City children sleep too much," she said, handing me a glass of warm milk with a skin on top.

After breakfast, we walked to the fields. She was seventy-six and walked faster than I did, her stick tapping the dusty path. She greeted every person we passed by name and asked about their goats, their children, their sick relatives. Everyone seemed to know her. A farmer stopped his tractor to touch her feet.

In the afternoon, she sat on her charpai and taught me to make roti on the tawa. Mine came out in the shape of Africa. She laughed until she had to wipe her eyes. Then she showed me a tin box under her bed. Inside were letters, yellow and soft, tied with a red thread.

"From your Nana," she said. "When he worked in the Gulf for eleven years. I couldn't read when the first one came. So I learnt, from the village schoolmaster's wife, so I could answer him myself."

I stared at her. I had never imagined my grandmother as a young woman learning her alphabet so she could write to her husband. I asked her to read one aloud. She did, slowly, her finger moving under the Urdu words. It was about rain, and a new buffalo, and how much he missed home.

That night, under a sky so full of stars that it looked crowded, I lay awake thinking. I had come expecting a boring day with an old woman. I left knowing that my grandmother had once been braver than I had ever needed to be.

model:
At half past four in the morning, Karachi sounds like a different city. My father and I left our flat in Gulshan-e-Iqbal to collect my aunt from the airport. Her flight from Jeddah was arriving at six, and Abbu wanted to "beat the traffic". There was no traffic to beat.

The streets were almost empty. Our car's headlights lit up shop shutters covered in painted adverts for tuition centres and mobile networks. A stray dog trotted along the pavement as if it owned the road. On University Road, a single bus rattled past, its lights glowing yellow, carrying a few sleepy workers to the early shift.

Near the Civic Centre, we stopped at a red light, although there was no one else at the crossing. "Rules are rules," Abbu said, and I rolled my eyes. In the silence I could hear the sea wind, which I never notice during the day.

On Shahrah-e-Faisal, the city began to wake. A man was sweeping the road with a long broom, raising clouds of dust in the streetlights. A boy on a bicycle carried a towering stack of newspapers. Outside a mosque, men in white caps were coming out from Fajr prayers, greeting each other quietly. At a corner, a tea stall was already open, its kettle steaming, and Abbu insisted we stop.

We sat on plastic stools and drank tea so sweet it made my teeth ache. The tea seller told us he had been opening the stall at four every morning for twenty years. "The city belongs to us at this time," he said with a grin. "By eight, it belongs to the cars."

We reached the airport just as the sky turned pink over the runway. My aunt came out pushing a trolley piled with zamzam water and dates.

I have lived in Karachi all my life. That morning, for the first time, I saw the people who wake it up.

prompt: Write about a time you were afraid of something and learned to face your fear.
task: Write a narrative of about 250-350 words in the first person. Describe the fear, the events that made you face it, and what you learned.
points: Opens by showing the fear vividly

model:
For as long as I could remember, I had been terrified of water. When I was six, I slipped into a canal near our village in Toba Tek Singh, and my uncle pulled me out by my collar. I didn't remember much, only the brown water closing over my head and the taste of mud.

After that, I refused to go near rivers, pools, even the sea on our one family trip to Karachi. My friends teased me gently. I laughed along, but I always found an excuse.

In my first year of college in Faisalabad, our physical education teacher, Sir Kamran, announced that every student had to pass a basic swimming test at the sports complex. I felt sick. I considered asking my father for a medical certificate. I even wrote one in my head.

On the first day at the pool, I stood at the edge while the others jumped in, shouting. The smell of chlorine made my stomach turn. Sir Kamran walked over. "You don't have to swim today," he said quietly. "Just sit on the steps with your feet in."

So I did. The next day, I stood in the shallow end up to my waist. The day after that, I let him hold my back while I floated, my heart thumping so hard I thought everyone could hear it. "The water wants to hold you up," he said. "You only sink when you fight it."

It took three weeks. There were days I gave up halfway through and went home angry. But on the last Friday, I pushed off from the wall and swam, clumsily, the whole length of the pool. When I reached the other side, I held on to the edge and laughed out loud. Some of my classmates clapped.

I learned that fear grows when you run from it and shrinks when you face it one small step at a time. I still don't love deep water, but it no longer owns me.

prompt: Write about a time you had to decide whether to report something wrong that you had seen.

From the window of the chemistry laboratory, Hamza saw two senior boys pushing a first-year student against the wall behind the canteen. One of them was holding the younger boy's phone above his head, laughing. The younger boy was trying not to cry.

It was the third time Hamza had seen it that month. The victim was a small, quiet boy called Arif, who had come to their college in Peshawar from a village in Swat. The seniors were well known: Danish and Junaid, both on the college football team, both popular, both friends of Hamza's elder cousin.

That evening, Hamza could not concentrate on his homework. If he reported them, everyone would know who had done it. His cousin would be angry. The football team might never accept him. If he stayed silent, Arif would face the same thing tomorrow, and the day after.

He spoke to his mother while she was folding clothes. He didn't use names. "If you saw someone being hurt, and helping made trouble for you, what would you do?"

She stopped folding. "What would you want someone to do if it were you?"

The next morning, Hamza went to the office of the discipline in-charge, Sir Tariq. His legs were shaking. He told him everything: the dates, the place, what he had seen. Sir Tariq listened without interrupting, then thanked him and promised to keep his name private.

Danish and Junaid were suspended for a week, and their parents were called. Hamza's cousin found out anyway and did not speak to him for a month. Some of the football players gave him cold looks.

But a week later, Arif sat down next to him in the library. "Someone told Sir Tariq," he said. "I don't know who. I wanted to thank them." Hamza said nothing, just pushed half his samosa across the table.

He had lost some friends. He had not lost his self-respect.

prompt: Write about a time you helped organise an event for a good cause.

It started with a notice on the board of our college in Mingora: the children's ward at the district hospital needed blankets before winter.

My friend Laiba read it aloud and said, "We should do something." We decided on a food stall at the college's annual spring fair. Five of us formed a team. Laiba handled the money. Asad, who was good at art, made the posters. Hira and Zoya planned the menu. I was in charge of "everything else", which meant asking permission, borrowing tables and persuading people.

The principal agreed, as long as we showed her the accounts afterwards. We collected small donations from our families to buy ingredients: chickpeas, potatoes, flour, tamarind. Our mothers taught us to make chana chaat and samosas in large quantities. My kitchen looked like a battlefield for two days.

The night before the fair, a problem: the gas cylinder we had borrowed was empty. Without it, we could not fry the samosas. We phoned everyone we knew. At ten o'clock, the watchman of our college, Lala Gul Khan, appeared at my gate carrying his own cylinder on his shoulder. "For the children," he said, and refused to take anything for it.

On the day, our stall was the busiest at the fair. Asad's posters, showing a child wrapped in a blanket, made people stop. Teachers bought plates for their whole families. A businessman from the town bought every remaining samosa and then paid double. By four o'clock we had sold out completely.

We counted the money three times in the principal's office: thirty-eight thousand rupees. With help from a wholesaler in the bazaar, it bought seventy warm blankets.

A week later, we delivered them to the hospital. One little girl wrapped herself up immediately and refused to let go.

I learned that a good cause needs more than good intentions. It needs planning, teamwork and, sometimes, a watchman with a gas cylinder.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the sentence: "I had only one chance to get it right."
task: Write a story of about 250-350 words, real or imagined, that begins with the given sentence. Show the build-up, the decisive moment and the outcome in a clear order.

I had only one chance to get it right. The district science exhibition in Jhelum allowed each team a single demonstration in front of the judges, and our project, a small solar-powered water pump, had failed twice during practice that week.

My partner, Rimsha, and I had spent two months building it in her garage. The idea was simple: a solar panel taken from an old garden lamp, a tiny motor from a broken toy car, and a pipe that could lift water from a bucket into a tray of seedlings. Farmers in her uncle's village spent hours carrying water by hand. We wanted to show there was another way.

On the morning of the exhibition, the sky was cloudy. Rimsha looked at it and groaned. "No sun, no pump," she said.

The hall was crowded with tables of robots, volcanoes and chemical reactions. We set up near a window, hoping for a gap in the clouds. Our turn was at eleven. At ten to eleven, the sky was still grey.

Then I remembered something our physics teacher had said: "Engineers plan for bad days." The night before, I had packed a small rechargeable battery and a switch, just in case. My hands shaking, I connected the battery to the circuit as a backup.

The judges arrived: two professors and an engineer from WAPDA. Rimsha explained the idea clearly while I watched the window. Just as I was about to switch to the battery, a thin beam of sunlight broke through the clouds and fell across the panel. The motor hummed. Water rose up the pipe and trickled into the seedlings.

"And if it's cloudy?" asked the engineer. I flicked the switch to show the battery. He nodded slowly and wrote something down.

We came second. Rimsha was disappointed, but I was not. The pump had worked, and we had been ready for both sun and cloud. One chance had been enough.

My elder brother Kamran and I had been fighting for months. He was twenty and studying engineering in Taxila; I was seventeen and, according to him, "useless". We argued about everything: the television remote, who would go to the market, whose turn it was to help our father in the shop.

One night in January, our parents went to a wedding in Wah, leaving us alone in our house in Attock. At about eleven, I woke to a strange smell. Smoke. I ran into the corridor and saw a thin grey cloud curling from under the kitchen door.

"Kamran!" I yelled.

He came running, half asleep. When he opened the kitchen door, we saw that the gas heater had set fire to the curtain beside it. Flames were climbing towards the wooden cupboard. For a second, we both froze.

Then something strange happened. We stopped being enemies. Kamran shouted, "Turn off the gas at the main!" and I ran outside to the meter without arguing. He pulled down the burning curtain with a wet towel and stamped on it. I came back with a bucket of water from the bathroom, and we threw it over the cupboard. Within three minutes, it was over. The kitchen was black and wet and smelt awful, but the fire was out.

We sat on the floor of the corridor, coughing and shaking. Kamran's hand was red where the curtain had touched it. I fetched ice and wrapped it in a cloth, and he let me hold it against his skin.

"You were quick," he said after a while.

"So were you," I replied.

When our parents came home, we told them about the heater, but not about how we had sat together until two in the morning, talking about things we had never discussed before: our fears, our futures, our grandfather.

The next day, we argued about the remote again. We never spoke about that night again, but we both remembered it.

On the day before Eid, nobody in our house has time for me. I am seven, and that is the problem with being the youngest.

In the morning, Ammi is in the kitchen making sheer khurma. The whole house smells of milk, cardamom and dates. She gives me one date and tells me to go away. Abbu has gone to the market for the third time because Dadi wants a different kind of vermicelli. My big sister Areeba is on the phone with her friends, talking about bangles, and she closes the door in my face.

At lunch, our cousins arrive from Sialkot. There are so many of them that I lose count at eleven. The grown-ups hug and say, "Mashallah, how tall!" to every child except me. My cousin Hassan, who is nine, says I am too small to play cricket. I sit on the stairs and feel sorry for myself.

In the afternoon, the ladies sit on the floor and put mehndi on each other's hands. I want some too. Areeba says I will smudge it. Phuppo says I will eat it. I am offended, because I only ate it last year.

Then something happens. The electricity goes and the house becomes dark and hot. Everyone groans. Dadi, who has been sitting quietly, calls me over. "Come," she whispers. "You hold the torch for me." While I shine it on her hands, she draws a tiny moon and a star on my palm with the mehndi cone. Nobody has a design like mine.

In the evening, everyone climbs to the roof to look for the Eid moon. The grown-ups argue about whether they can see it. I see it first, a thin silver line over the water tank, and I shout so loudly that the whole street hears me. Everybody cheers.

At night, Dadi kisses my mehndi hand. I sleep with it held carefully above the blanket. Being the youngest isn't so bad after all.

prompt: Write about a day when you had to take responsibility for your home or family because the adults were away.

model:
"You're in charge," my mother said, handing me a list and a fold of money. "Back by eight." She and my father were taking my grandfather to a specialist in Multan, leaving me, at sixteen, with my twin brothers, aged ten, and our house in Vehari.

The list looked simple: give the boys breakfast, make sure they do their homework, buy flour and vegetables, cook rice for dinner, lock the gate at night. By nine o'clock, I had already failed the first task. The twins wanted parathas; I could only make eggs. They ate them, grumbling, then started a pillow fight that knocked a glass off the table.

At eleven, I took them to the market. Ali disappeared while I was paying for tomatoes. My heart stopped. For five terrible minutes, I searched the stalls, calling his name, imagining what I would tell my mother. I found him at the end of the street watching a man repair a motorbike, completely unaware of my panic. I didn't shout. I just held his hand so tightly all the way home that he complained.

In the afternoon, I made them sit at the table for homework. Usman cried over his maths, so I sat with him and drew the sums as apples and bananas, the way my mother did for me once. He finished, and even said thank you.

The crisis came at six: the rice burnt. The whole kitchen filled with smoke. I opened every window, threw the pot outside and, feeling defeated, phoned our neighbour, Auntie Rehana. Ten minutes later she arrived with a dish of daal and fresh rotis. "Everyone burns their first rice," she said.

When my parents returned, the boys were asleep, the dishes were washed and the gate was locked. My mother looked at the list, then at me, and hugged me.

I learned that day that being in charge doesn't mean nothing goes wrong. It means you deal with whatever does.

The interview for the scholarship was at ten o'clock in Islamabad. I lived in a small town near Chakwal, and the only way to get there in time was the six o'clock coaster from the main chowk.

My mother woke me at half past four and stood over me while I ate a paratha I could not taste. My father walked with me to the chowk in the dark, carrying my file of certificates as if it were made of glass. "Speak slowly," he said. "And look at them when you answer."

The coaster was packed. I sat squashed between a soldier going back to his unit and a woman with a basket of eggs on her lap. The road wound through the salt hills, and every bump made the woman grip her basket and me grip my file. I tried to revise the answers I had prepared, but the words kept jumbling in my head.

Near Kallar Kahar, the coaster stopped. A truck had broken down across the road. Twenty minutes passed. I kept looking at my watch, imagining the door of the interview room closing. I had bought twenty tomato seedlings from the nursery, and our backyard was small. So I planted them all in two tight rows, each plant barely a hand's width from the next.

For the first three weeks, everything looked perfect. The plants grew tall and green, and I wrote proud entries in my diary. Dada Jan came out every morning, looked at them, shook his head and said nothing more. I took his silence as approval.

Then the monsoon rains came. After a week of damp, cloudy weather, I noticed brown spots on the lower leaves. Within days, the spots had spread from plant to plant. The leaves curled and fell. Half the plants began to wilt.

I ran to my grandfather. He bent down and turned over a leaf. "Blight," he said. "When plants are too close, the leaves stay wet. The disease jumps from one to the next."

The road ahead was blocked, and the sun was beginning to set. A landslide had brought down half the mountainside onto the Karakoram Highway, somewhere between Chilas and Gilgit, and a line of buses, trucks and cars stretched back behind us for a kilometre.

My mother, my younger brother Faisal and I were travelling to my uncle's house in Gilgit for my cousin's wedding. Our driver, a quiet man called Sher Ali, switched off the engine and climbed out to talk to the other drivers. When he came back, his face was serious. "The machines can't come until morning," he said. "We'll have to stay the night here."

My mother looked at the darkening mountains and pulled her shawl tighter. There was no village nearby, no hotel, only rocks, the roaring Indus far below, and a cold wind that grew stronger every minute. Faisal, who was eleven, began asking whether there were wolves.

Sher Ali did not seem worried. He walked to a tea stall that had appeared, as if by magic, at the roadside, set up by a man from a nearby hamlet with a kettle and a gas burner. Soon, travellers were gathering around it. A truck driver from Swat lit a small fire with dry branches. A family from Lahore shared their packets of biscuits. He first came through this gate when he was five, holding his mother's hand so tightly that his knuckles were white. He cried every morning for a month. I used to give him a toffee from my pocket and tell him that the gate was magic: it only let in brave boys. He would wipe his face and march in.

This morning, the boys arrived in pressed uniforms, laughing too loudly, the way young people do when they are sad. There were photographs, speeches in the hall, and the headmaster's long prayer. I listened from the gate.

At one o'clock, they began to leave. Junaid came last. He is taller than me now, with the beginnings of a moustache. He stopped at the gate and stood there for a moment, saying nothing.
